posts.note: Satirical 'fan fiction' legal brief: Dobbs ended the federal privacy right, so federal privacy class actions against Cerebral fail and HIPAA should go. Logged the conditional legal predictions and the California-standards call with satire noted.
Science explainer on benzodiazepines; only an own-publication plan (PBM piece and Carelon companion piece).

Long PBM / fiduciary-duty essay. Calls about litigation outcomes, insiders taking Big Health down, deductible trend, revenue extrapolation, the cost-plus card, own-publication plans, and one quoted CVS CEO forecast (own_claim false).
Anti-VC essay; mostly advice and present analysis. Logged aphoristic rules and generic conditional claims with notes; 'should/stop' advice not logged.
Opinion on NPD stigma; one hedged conditional about treatment reducing abuse and one weak future-research line quoted from the author's own lab abstract.
Richard III parody poem about Clarence Thomas; one prediction that disclosure failures 'will nail him', logged as sincere inside parody framing.
Video promo; present-tense growth claims and subscription pitch only. 'you're probably not gonna read it' is a reader-behaviour quip, not logged.

statements.quote: Every state can craft its own privacy laws— except, practically, California will dictate the standards across all healthcare products given the size of the market.
statements.context: In a satirical 'fan fiction' brief arguing that Dobbs ended the federal right to privacy and that HIPAA should be scrapped, the author predicts that, with privacy law left to the states, California will set the de facto privacy standard for all healthcare products because of its market size.
statements.note: Conditional on HIPAA being scrapped / no federal privacy right. Satirical post, but the California-standard claim reads sincere (fuel-efficiency precedent cited).

statements.quote: This is already standard operating procedure for the state of California when it comes to fuel efficiency standards, and I would be shocked if they didn't take a swing at Texas in this manner.
statements.context: Same passage: the author expects California to use state privacy law-making to counter Texas (abortion-enforcement access to health data), as it does with fuel-efficiency standards.
statements.confidence_phrase: I would be shocked if they didn't
statements.note: Conditional on a state-level privacy regime replacing HIPAA; satirical post.

statements.quote: Overturn HIPAA and sure, Cerebral escapes the federal court headache, but now has to face the music in state courts.
statements.context: Conditional legal prediction: if HIPAA / the federal privacy right is overturned, the federal class action against Cerebral (Facebook pixel tracking) fails, and Cerebral would instead face privacy suits in state courts.
statements.note: Conditional inside satirical legal fan fiction; the author says of the theory 'I think this holds up'.

statements.quote: This implies eliminating HIPAA, and without a federal right to privacy, class action lawsuits on privacy matters in federal court would be inapplicable.
statements.context: Core legal thesis: applying Justice Alito's Dobbs logic, healthcare privacy becomes a state matter; without a federal privacy right, federal privacy class actions (such as the one against Cerebral and other telehealth companies) would not be viable.
statements.note: Conditional legal reasoning presented as a sincere theory within a satirical frame.

statements.quote: Honestly, privacy is over. Privacy is a terrible legal framework with which to protect healthcare information.
statements.context: Footnote 1: the author declares privacy finished as a legal framework for protecting health information and argues property law is the better framework.
statements.note: Present-tense 'is dead'-style negative call; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: By smashing HIPAA to bits, via Cerebral's court case, we can lock down our personal data like a vault. And that, my friends, is a future we can all feel good about.
statements.context: Closing vision: if HIPAA is dismantled through the Cerebral litigation, health data could be protected by encryption and property-style rights instead of privacy law.
statements.note: Conditional vision / proposal with weak predictive reading; satirical frame. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: I'm not a lawyer. I don't even play one on TV. I do some testimony in expert witness gigs. But I think this holds up.
statements.context: Close of footnote 1: the author asserts that his legal theory (no federal privacy right after Dobbs, so federal privacy class actions against Cerebral fail) would hold up.
statements.note: Belief that the legal argument would survive scrutiny; borderline forecast about court treatment.

statements.quote: I’m working on a very difficult to write piece about pharmacy benefit managers and a companion piece about Carelon, and a few other pieces (108 drafts, and 3 books in draft)
statements.context: Opening housekeeping of a science short: the author announces upcoming newsletter pieces on pharmacy benefit managers and on Carelon, plus books in draft.
statements.note: Own publication plan; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I find it motivating, and I will do more ambitious writing if you reinforce my behavior.
statements.context: Intro to the PBM essay: conditional own-plan to produce more ambitious writing if readers subscribe and share.
statements.note: Own-activity conditional; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Finally, I will explain the legal strategy that I see starting to solve this problem for all.
statements.context: Roadmap sentence of the PBM essay; embeds the author's view that a legal strategy (fiduciary-duty enforcement under the CAA 2021 and ERISA) is starting to solve the PBM racket problem for everyone.
statements.note: Within-post promise plus an implicit expectation that the legal strategy will work; borderline.

statements.quote: More is coming on that stupid saga, but I will mention it is not in my financial interest to pay lawyers to harass me.
statements.context: After describing a threatening letter from a Troutman Pepper partner over his complaints about his health plan, the author promises more newsletter coverage of the dispute.
statements.note: Own publication plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: You might never meet the deductible— 50% never do each year , and climbing.
statements.context: Argument that premiums do not count toward deductibles: the author states that half of plan members never meet their deductible each year and that this share is rising.
statements.note: Trend claim: the share of members who never meet the deductible is increasing.

statements.quote: What does a company that makes hundreds of billions and is growing at 8.8% per year have as a product?
statements.context: Next to a Grand View Research PBM market chart: the author restates the PBM market growth rate as 8.8% per year.
statements.note: Restates a market-research CAGR (likely a projection) in present tense; weak forecast, logged for recall.

statements.quote: If one were paying for interplanetary travel, the trip from Earth to Saturn, at $1 a meter, would be affordable next year if costs go up at current rates — it’s 1.38 trillion meters away.
statements.context: Scale illustration after citing 2022 Big Insurance revenue of $1.25 trillion: at current growth rates, Big Health revenue would reach about $1.38 trillion next year.
statements.confidence_phrase: would be affordable next year if costs go up at current rates
statements.note: Humorous framing (the author calls the space comparison an exaggeration), but the numeric extrapolation (revenue of at least $1.38T next year at current growth) reads sincere.

statements.quote: We can never get there. This “never” is important to understand; just like the mob, Big Health really can not stop putting the squeeze on you.
statements.context: Argument that 'value' rhetoric is hollow: Big Health companies will never reach value and cannot stop extracting money because of their fiduciary duty to shareholders.
statements.note: Negative structural call about payer / PBM behaviour.

statements.quote: The Culture of Obedience, endless doublespeak, complexity, and mind-numbing profits can’t be undone by outsiders. It’s too powerful.
statements.context: RICO analogy: the author asserts outsiders cannot dismantle the Big Health / PBM system; only insiders using its own logic can.
statements.note: Negative call about who can change the system; paired with the next statement.

statements.quote: The Big Health Mafia used complexity to shake us down. In turn, it will be taken down by those who ran the scam.
statements.context: Prediction that former insiders (Wendell Potter, Dave Chase, Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Drugs, ERISA lawyers such as Doug Aldeen) will bring down the Big Health / PBM system.
statements.note: Open-ended, no date.

statements.quote: Mobsters eventually turned into rats for less. Are the contract killers working at PBMs less tough than Junior Soprano? I can’t wait to find out.
statements.context: After laying out ERISA criminal penalties (up to 10 years) as the 'health benefits version of RICO', the author implies PBM insiders will turn informant under criminal exposure.
statements.confidence_phrase: I can’t wait to find out
statements.note: Implicit expectation phrased as a rhetorical question; borderline.

statements.quote: A legal framework where people who aren’t Made Guys in the Big Health Mafia—that is, every employer and anyone who exerts a coercive influence in the protection racket in America— have PERSONAL and plausibly CATASTROPHIC liability, both civil and criminal.
statements.context: The author's summary of the CAA 2021 fiduciary rule and ERISA penalties: employers and brokers now face personal, potentially catastrophic civil and criminal liability.
statements.note: Present legal characterization with the forward implication that this liability will be enforced; borderline.

statements.quote: Meanwhile, that cost-plus pharmacy card will work at most pharmacies.
statements.context: Closing practical advice: the Rethinking Heroes / CapitalRx cost-plus discount card will be accepted at most pharmacies.
statements.note: The author built the first version of the card and works with Jerry Ashton; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: you can ask your pharmacist to tell you how much your prescription would be “with your insurance” and its co-pay, and how much it would be not using your insurance with the above cost plus discount card. The answer is likely to surprise you!
statements.context: Claim that the cost-plus card cash price will often be lower than the insurance co-pay (the 'clawback').
statements.note: Generic expectation about price comparisons; the author is affiliated with the card.

statements.quote: They failed, but others will sue and win. It’s already heating up with Perez, Ca 2021 enforcement and regulatory scrutiny.
statements.context: Footnote 9 on the health plan's late legal reply: the author predicts other plaintiffs will sue Big Health plans / PBMs over fiduciary breaches and win, citing rising CAA 2021 enforcement.
statements.note: Litigation-outcome call; 'Perez' appears to reference an ERISA case.

statements.quote: The character count on the transcript of those calls is over 30,000 words. I might publish it as a hard-bound book to be an art nerd.
statements.context: Footnote 6: the author may publish the transcript of his compliance-department calls as a book.
statements.note: Own publication musing; CONTROL candidate; low value.

statements.quote: but I imagine the discovery, in that case, is most of the evidence needed for this one, vastly reducing the cost of the litigation
statements.context: Footnote 12 on Ford's Sherman Act antitrust suit against Blue Cross plans: the author expects discovery from the earlier $2.7b class action settlement to supply most of the evidence and cut Ford's litigation costs.
statements.note: Litigation-process call.

statements.quote: “We welcome competition ... expect more of it in the years to come and are confident that we ourselves are key disruptors,” Merlo CVS CEO said.
statements.context: Quoted as an example of Big Health doublespeak: CVS CEO Larry Merlo expects more PBM competition in the coming years.
statements.note: Third-party forecast quoted skeptically; the author does not adopt it (own_claim false). The ' ... ' is in the source text.

statements.quote: II. Payers Demand Pilots That Will Fail
statements.context: Item II of the author's 'Rule of the House of Odds' for healthcare businesses (a House of God parody): pilots demanded by payers will fail.
statements.note: Aphoristic generic rule; low resolvability.

statements.quote: VI. There is no healthcare play that can succeed absent a guaranteed government payer
statements.context: Item VI of the same rules: no healthcare business can succeed without a guaranteed government payer.
statements.confidence_phrase: There is no healthcare play that can succeed
statements.note: Aphoristic generic negative call.

statements.quote: The expectations venture investors have are that they're going to want you to grow fast, and that means you're gonna have a very hard time maintaining the kind of quality that creates sustainable business model.
statements.context: Argument against raising venture capital for healthcare companies: VC growth pressure will erode care quality and business sustainability.
statements.note: Generic conditional claim about VC-backed healthcare startups.

statements.quote: They will also expect to a burn rate. This means you spend more money than you make. This also means you create a business that fails the second the necessary extra cash dries up.
statements.context: Same argument: VC-expected burn rates create healthcare businesses that fail when outside funding stops.
statements.note: Generic conditional claim; coder may treat as truism.

statements.quote: If we think narcissism is related to abuse, treating narcissism, and creating help that is understood as helpful to those suffering from NPD? It may lead to less abuse of others! Insults to potential abusers— adding a pejorative or even an accurate label—can't help.
statements.context: Opinion piece against the phrase 'narcissistic abuse': treating narcissistic personality disorder may reduce abuse of others, while stigmatizing labels cannot help.
statements.note: Hedged conditional clinical claim.

statements.quote: This is an area that can direct future NPD research to develop a comprehensive approach to NPD management.
statements.context: Quoted from the author's own lab's paper on clinician attitudes toward NPD (group therapy seen as helpful but rarely offered); points to a future research direction.
statements.note: Quoted from the author's own published abstract; weak predictive content; logged for recall.

statements.quote: The inappropriate lack of disclosures of a sitting Supreme Court Justice will nail him.
statements.context: Closing line of a Richard III parody poem about Clarence Thomas's financial-disclosure controversies: the author predicts the disclosure failures will bring consequences for Thomas. Lead-in is conditional: 'if Clarence be as influenceable as his peers are wealthy'.
statements.note: Parody framing; the expectation of consequences reads sincere. Not a healthcare call.
